author: haiku
reason: A explains up front why the design is shaped this way (the 60-second request limit, retries that keep no progress, and therefore checkpointed parts), defines every term it relies on, gives a table of the stored state and a summary of what happens on each failure, so a newcomer can build the whole mental model from it; B is shorter and easier to skim but leaves more of the mechanism implied or deferred.

author: haiku
reason: B opens by explaining why the design has two paths and a resumable job. It then gives a full table of the stored fields and ends with a table of what happens on each failure, so a newcomer can find their way and check the design, even though it is longer and more complex than A's tighter description of a simpler design.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the existing stack before the design: the 60 s request limit, 512 MB workers, how attempts and retries work, at-least-once delivery, multipart rules and bucket lifecycle. It also says why there are two paths, so a newcomer can see why each step is built the way it is, while B leaves most of those limits unstated even though it is tighter and has a handy failure table.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the better handover for someone new to the stack: before the steps, it explains the constraints the design depends on, such as the 60-second request limit, the 512 MB workers, the queue's at-least-once retry behaviour, the multipart upload and bucket rules, and keyset paging, and it says why there are two paths. A is tighter, but it uses those limits without introducing them, so a newcomer has to guess why the design looks the way it does.

author: haiku
reason: I would rather be handed A: it spells out how the limiter actually works (the Lua script, how windowIndex and the counter key are built, where Retry-After comes from, what the 50 ms deadline covers, what happens on a backend timeout) and lists more unknowns honestly, while B is easier to read but leaves the counter design, Key Service failures and Redis failover vague.

author: haiku
reason: B is longer, but it explains why the steps run in this order, defines every term a newcomer would hit (Key Service, Lua EVAL, PTTL, windowIndex) and shows the actual check-and-increment script, so an outsider can rebuild the whole design from it; A is tighter but leaves more to inference.

author: sonnet
reason: A walks a newcomer through the whole request path in numbered steps tied to the diagram, defines the unfamiliar pieces (Redis, the Lua script, fail open), places the cache in the gateway where it actually is, and covers Key Service and backend failures that B leaves out or calls out of scope, so it explains how the system works more completely and with less ambiguity.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I'd rather be handed: it explains the parts an outsider wouldn't know (what the Key Service is, how Redis is set up, what a Lua script guarantees), walks through the flow step by step against the diagram, and covers more failure cases, such as Key Service outages, backend 502/504 errors and lost Redis keys, giving the reason behind each choice and marking which choices are its own assumptions.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is the one I would rather be handed, because it starts with the existing system's constraints, defines nearly every term it uses, and explains how writes, relays, erasure, ids and failures work before the rollout steps; B leaves references such as `jobs:dead`, the 5-retry cap and the "migration layer" unexplained and scatters how the system runs across its checklist.

author: haiku
reason: B gives an outsider what A takes for granted: the baseline (row count, load, replica lag, how erasure works, flag refresh and caching, why app.jobs is unsafe), separate sections on how writes, erasure and ids work before and after the switch, and a failure table, so the system makes sense on its own, while A relies on unexplained context such as the 30 s refresh, the 90 s limit, jobs:dead and the 5-retry cap.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is longer, but it explains more of what an outsider needs: where `version` comes from, how flags are cached and drift between instances, why the fence and version rule make overlapping copies safe, how read misses behave before and after the switch, and a failure table, so you can rebuild the system's behaviour from it, while B is more compact and leaves more of that reasoning unstated.

author: sonnet
reason: For a newcomer, B explains more. It starts with a five-phase overview and says what already exists (the version column, the Postgres pool, the Redis queue's flaws), defines every flag and fence in plain terms, gives the reasons behind subtle rules such as a read miss being final after the switch, and ends with a table of failures and their results. A is tighter but assumes more prior knowledge, and its delete and backfill-baseline reasoning is denser.

author: haiku
reason: Document A shows exactly how double charges are prevented: claim rows with a unique key, the claimed, charged and released states, the drain step and how the handoff works. It also says where each piece of state lives. Document B is easier to skim but stays vague on that core mechanism, leaning on a proposed rollback marker and a loose "the ledger enforces one key".

author: haiku
reason: Document A gives a newcomer a clean mental model in one pass: a short glossary, one rollback sub-machine, linear steps that each say how they start, what they keep and how they fail, and a compact failures table. Document B is more rigorous about claim-row mechanics, but it duplicates the rollback states in its diagram and buries the core flow under dense detail and twelve open questions.
